cards.text: Ezekiel, a prophet, gets a new word from the LORD in the twelfth year, on the first day of the twelfth month. The LORD has had words for Pharaoh king of Egypt before (Ezekiel 31:2), and here He goes again. This time God tells Ezekiel to take up a lament for Pharaoh and say it right to him.
The lament starts with Pharaoh's picture: he's like a lion among the nations. Friend, MY first introduction was a sticker that said 25 cents.

cards.question: In the lament, Pharaoh is like a lion among the nations. Out in the seas, he's like a ___.
In the lament, Pharaoh is like a monster in the seas. True or false: he keeps his rivers calm and his streams clear.

cards.text: He thrashes around in his rivers, churning up the water with his feet and muddying the streams. Then the Lord GOD speaks, and friend, this monster is about to meet his match.

cards.question: Pharaoh is like a monster splashing around in the water. What does the Lord GOD say He'll spread over him?

cards.text: God says a company of many peoples will draw Pharaoh up in His net. The biggest thing in the river, hauled up in a NET.

cards.question: Once Pharaoh is hauled out of the water in God's net, where does God say He'll leave him?
Out in the open field, God says no creature will come near Pharaoh.

cards.text: God says the birds will settle on him and the beasts of the earth will eat their fill. He'll put Pharaoh's flesh on the mountains, fill the valleys with his remains, and drench the land with his blood all the way to the mountains.

cards.question: When God extinguishes Pharaoh, He turns to the sky over him. What does God say happens to the sun, the moon and the stars?

cards.text: God says every shining light in the heavens will go dark over Pharaoh, and He'll bring darkness on his land. My night sky out back is still waiting on most of its stars, and I'd PANIC if one went out.
God says He'll trouble the hearts of many peoples when He brings Pharaoh's destruction among the nations, even in countries Pharaoh doesn't know. Word of this fall is traveling FAR.

cards.question: God says He'll brandish His sword before many peoples. How will their kings react to Pharaoh's fall?

cards.text: On the day Pharaoh falls, each king will tremble every moment for his life. It's like when the big boss gets walked out of the building, and suddenly the whole office shows up EARLY.

cards.question: Then God names whose sword is coming for Pharaoh: 'The sword of the king of ___ will come against you!'

cards.text: That's Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Ezekiel 30:10). God says Egypt's hordes will fall by the swords of the mighty, the most ruthless of all nations.

cards.question: The most ruthless of all nations come against Egypt. What does God say they'll ravage?

cards.text: God says He'll slaughter all of Egypt's cattle beside the abundant waters. Remember how Pharaoh was like a monster muddying the streams with his feet?

cards.question: After Egypt's cattle are slaughtered, God says human feet and cattle hooves will keep stirring up Egypt's waters.
With nothing stirring them up, God says He'll let Egypt's waters ___ and make her rivers flow like oil.

cards.text: The thrashing is over. God says He'll make Egypt a desolation, empty it of all that filled it, and strike down all who live there.

cards.question: When God makes Egypt a desolation, what does He say they will know?

cards.text: And it all comes back around to the lament. God says this is the song that will be chanted over Egypt and all her multitudes.

cards.question: God says the daughters of the nations will chant this lament over Egypt.

findings.problem: "and here He goes again" is a flippant, exasperated idiom aimed at God. It reads as a light jab at the LORD rather than a joke Papa Dorin makes about himself.

rule.text: His humor never targets God, Jesus, Scripture or the Marriage Supper.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess the next word of the poetic line ("like a ___" in the seas), and nothing on the earlier cards lets them reason it out. The answers are also different kinds of thing. "monster" is the only creature, set against an object (ship) and a person (fisherman), so the right answer stands out as the only match for "lion."

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The answers are not the same kind of thing: a creature, an object and a person.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: One story card carries three separate things: birds and beasts eating (v4), flesh on the mountains and remains in the valleys (v5), and blood drenching the land (v6).

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: "Word of this fall is traveling FAR" adds an explanation of how the destruction reaches "countries you do not know" (news spreading). The text leaves that connection open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The baker has nothing to reason from, so this is a guessed detail of the line's wording ("ravage the ___ of Egypt"). The right answer also stands out. "The pride of Egypt" is abstract and sounds more like the Bible, while the wrong answers "The temples of Egypt" and "The ships of Egypt" are concrete.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The right answer "That I am the LORD" stands out. It is the only answer in God's first-person voice and the only one with the familiar biblical phrase. "That Babylon is mighty" and "That Pharaoh was a fool" are third-person and plainer.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The card calls the lament "the song," but verse 16 calls it "the lament."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.
